summary: Describes how to use a SAML 2.0 bearer assertion with OAuth 2.0, both to request an access token and to authenticate a client. It is a profile of the assertion framework in RFC 7521, tying existing SAML-based identity systems to OAuth.

eli5.summary: A big company already hands out signed badges in one format. This document explains how a different website can accept that kind of badge and give you a visitor pass in exchange.

questions: use saml to get an oauth access token
what is a saml bearer assertion
how to get an oauth access token with saml
subtitle: How a signed SAML assertion can be traded for an OAuth 2.0 access token, or used to prove who a client is.

tldr.problem: Organizations that already use SAML 2.0 to share identity information want to reach OAuth 2.0 protected resources without a new user approval step at the authorization server.
tldr.mechanism: A SAML 2.0 Bearer Assertion is sent to the OAuth token endpoint, base64url-encoded, either as an authorization grant or as client credentials. The server validates issuer, audience, subject, expiry and signature.
tldr.outcome: SAML-based trust relationships can be bridged into OAuth 2.0. Replay protection is optional, and the two uses can be combined or used separately.

today: RFC 7522 is a Proposed Standard from May 2015. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC, and it builds on the framework in RFC 7521.

sections.title: Bridging SAML and OAuth
sections.content:
SAML 2.0 is an XML-based framework for sharing identity and security information across security domains. Its Assertion is an XML security token, normally issued by an Identity Provider and consumed by a Service Provider.

In OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749), a client uses an authorization grant to get an access token from an authorization server. OAuth allows new grant types and new client authentication methods. This RFC profiles the assertion framework in RFC 7521 to define a grant type and a client authentication method that use a SAML 2.0 Bearer Assertion.

The RFC says the client can use an existing trust relationship, expressed by the assertion, without a direct user approval step at the authorization server. How the client first obtains the assertion is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Some places already use signed badges to say who you are. This lets a different place trust the same badge and hand you what you need.

sections.title: Two Separate Uses of an Assertion
sections.content:
The assertion can serve two roles. As an authorization grant, it is exchanged for an access token. As client authentication, it is an alternative way for the client to prove itself to the token endpoint.

These are orthogonal and separable. They can be used together or separately. Client assertion authentication must be used with some grant type to make a complete request. An assertion grant may be used with or without client authentication or identification, and whether it is needed is a policy decision of the authorization server. If client credentials are present, the server MUST validate them.
sections.eli5: The badge can be used to get a pass, or just to show who you are when asking for something else. You can do either one, or both.

sections.title: HTTP Parameters for the Assertion
sections.content:
For a grant, the request sets grant_type to urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:saml2-bearer. The assertion parameter holds a single SAML 2.0 Assertion and MUST NOT hold more than one. The scope parameter may be used, and client_id is only needed when the chosen client authentication relies on it.

For client authentication, client_assertion_type is urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:saml2-bearer, and client_assertion MUST contain a single assertion.

In both cases the XML is encoded with base64url as defined in RFC 4648, with padding bits set to zero. The encoded data must not be line wrapped and must not include = pad characters. For the grant these are MUST NOT requirements. For client authentication they are SHOULD NOT.
sections.eli5: The badge is squashed into a plain string of letters so it can travel in an ordinary web request. Two fields say what kind of badge it is and carry the badge itself.

sections.title: What the Server Must Check
sections.content:
The authorization server MUST validate the assertion against a list of rules. Extra restrictions are at the server's discretion.

  • The Issuer element holds a unique identifier of the issuer.
  • A Conditions element with an AudienceRestriction and Audience must name the authorization server. The server MUST reject an assertion that does not contain its own identity as audience. The token endpoint URL MAY be used as an audience value.
  • A Subject must identify the principal. For client authentication the subject MUST be the client_id.
  • The assertion MUST have an expiry, via NotOnOrAfter on Conditions or on a suitable SubjectConfirmationData.
  • The subject MUST have a SubjectConfirmation with method urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:cm:bearer. Its Recipient, when present, must match the token endpoint URL the assertion was delivered to.
  • The assertion MUST be digitally signed or have a Message Authentication Code applied by the issuer, and invalid ones MUST be rejected.

Expired assertions are rejected, subject to allowable clock skew. The server MAY prevent replay by remembering used ID values for as long as the assertion would be valid. If the issuer directly authenticated the subject, the assertion SHOULD carry one AuthnStatement. If the client acts autonomously for the subject, it SHOULD NOT, and the client SHOULD be identified in the confirmation. Encrypted elements MAY appear in place of plaintext ones.
sections.eli5: The server is a careful doorman. It checks who made the badge, that the badge is meant for this door, who it is about, that it has not expired and that the signature is real.

sections.title: Error Responses
sections.content:
If an assertion used as a grant is not valid, including when its subject confirmation requirements cannot be met, the server builds an OAuth 2.0 error response with the error value invalid_grant. It MAY add detail in error_description or error_uri. The RFC example is a 400 Bad Request with the description "Audience validation failed".

If an assertion used for client authentication is not valid, the error value MUST be invalid_client.
sections.eli5: If the badge is no good, the doorman says no and, if he wants, tells you why.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC shows an assertion issued and signed by the Identity Provider https://saml-idp.example.com. Its subject is brian@example.com, who authenticated by a digital signature with a key validated through an X.509 Public Key Infrastructure. The audience is https://saml-sp.example.net, and the recipient is the token endpoint https://authz.example.net/token.oauth2.

The client then sends the base64url-encoded assertion in a POST to that endpoint with the grant type above. A separate example shows an authorization code grant request that also carries a client_assertion.
sections.eli5: The RFC walks through one full badge and one request, so you can see every piece in place.

sections.title: Interoperability, Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Both sides must agree out of band on issuer and audience values, the token endpoint location, the signing key, one-time use restrictions, maximum assertion lifetime, and subject and attribute requirements. RSA-SHA256 from RFC 6931 is a mandatory-to-implement XML signature algorithm.

The security considerations of RFC 7521, RFC 6749 and the SAML security document all apply. Replay protection is not mandated and is optional. Because an assertion may hold privacy-sensitive data, it should only travel over encrypted channels such as TLS. Subjects and attributes can be encrypted to the authorization server, and deployments should include only the minimum information needed.
sections.eli5: Both sides must agree on the details beforehand. Badges should travel in a sealed envelope and carry only what is needed.
